data.title: Shinde orders crackdown on illegal hoardings in Thane, seeks new ad policy
data.description:
Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde has directed civic officials in Thane to crack down on unauthorised hoardings that are defacing the city and to frame a new advertising policy, officials said on Saturday.

Shinde, who is also the Guardian Minister of the district, has directed Thane Municipal Corporation (TMC) Commissioner Saurabh Rao to launch a special drive and impose heavy penalties and criminal cases against violators, an official release by his office said.

Alongside the enforcement drive, Shinde also suggested that the civic body formulate its own comprehensive new hoarding policy.

Under the proposed policy, he directed the administration to identify suitable locations across the city for installing digital hoardings and allow authorised advertisements against prescribed fees.

 

He noted that regulating outdoor advertising through digital hoardings would not only curb visual clutter but also boost the Thane Municipal Corporation's revenue.

data.title: OpenAI accuses Apple of undermining supplier relationships, unfair hiring
data.description:
By Erik Larson
 
The trade-secrets fight between OpenAI and Apple Inc. is widening, with the artificial intelligence company accusing the iPhone maker of undermining its supplier relationships and using unfair employment agreements to prevent talent from jumping ship. 
OpenAI made the allegations in counterclaims against Apple on Friday in federal court in San Jose, California. The filing also accuses Apple of stealing OpenAI’s trade secrets, transforming the lawsuit Apple brought earlier against OpenAI into a two-way battle over the companies’ intellectual property.
 
The case has overshadowed OpenAI’s bid to sell its own devices, a move that would put it in competition with the iPhone maker. Former Apple design guru Jony Ive is helping the AI company develop a family of products, starting with what’s expected to be a doughnut-shaped smart speaker.
 
 
“Apple has responded to OpenAI’s anticipated entry into the hardware market by unlawfully pressuring vendors not to work with OpenAI and using expansive employment restraints to limit OpenAI’s access to talented engineers,” OpenAI said in the filing. “Apple’s power over suppliers and engineers cannot lawfully be used to exclude competing purchasers and employers from the market.”
 
Apple in July sued OpenAI and Tang Tan, the AI company’s chief hardware officer, alleging the ChatGPT maker orchestrated a campaign to steal trade secrets via job candidates and hires from Apple. The companies had earlier collaborated to integrate ChatGPT directly into iPhone, iPad and Mac software, only to see that relationship cool more recently.
 
Apple argues that its lawsuit includes extensive evidence that OpenAI employees used a stolen Apple-issued laptop to access its information and exploited a rare, previously-unknown authentication bug to access the iPhone maker’s shared network. Apple also claims OpenAI asked job candidates still working for Apple to bring “actual parts” from Apple to interviews.
 
Apple said OpenAI’s counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of the phone maker’s lawsuit, “in which OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple’s confidential information.”
 
“This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple’s secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products — not about inadvertent retention of Apple information,” the Cupertino, California-based company said in a statement.
 
OpenAI also alleges Apple unfairly pressures industry suppliers to “identify their OpenAI projects and the names, locations, and assignments of workers with Apple experience.” 
 
Apple then seeks to exclude workers with OpenAI experience from doing further work for the iPhone maker, effectively discouraging suppliers from committing workers to OpenAI projects, according to the filing.
 
Another industry supplier that provides specialist finishing services moved its manufacturing work for OpenAI products to the night shift to avoid overlapping with work for Apple, increasing costs for OpenAI, according to the filing. The supplier did so under pressure from Apple, OpenAI says.
 
“Suppliers have expressed fear of losing Apple business and have moved or rescheduled meetings with OpenAI to avoid Apple seeing them,” according to OpenAI’s counterclaims. “Other suppliers have told OpenAI personnel that they must be cautious about devoting staff, production resources, or managerial attention to OpenAI.”
 
OpenAI has denied wrongdoing and has asked a judge to toss out Apple’s lawsuit. In October, OpenAI voluntarily agreed not to use trade secrets that Apple claims were stolen when a judge said he was likely to issue an order to that effect.
 
OpenAI alleges in its counterclaims that a former employee — who had left Apple for OpenAI but later returned to Apple — had sent “over a hundred highly confidential files” about at least one unreleased OpenAI device to personal accounts. The files included images of unreleased hardware, engineering and manufacturing data and supplier information, OpenAI said.
 
In response, Apple said it has policies in place to prevent the use of confidential information from former employers and that it found no evidence to substantiate OpenAI’s claims.
 
The new counterclaims also accuse Apple of using unfair employment agreements to prevent its engineers from leaving for OpenAI. The AI company is challenging provisions that bar former Apple employees from soliciting or recruiting Apple workers for one year. 
 
OpenAI argues that Apple’s intellectual property agreements, or IPAs, which employees must sign, use an overly broad definition of the company’s private information. The agreements essentially cover all nonpublic information that employees learn from the iPhone maker, even if it isn’t a trade secret, unfairly restricting former employees’ professional skills and putting them at risk of being sued, OpenAI says.
 
Apple’s lawsuit names a former iPhone engineer, Chang Liu, who joined OpenAI in January. Apple claims he accessed confidential hardware-related files over a period of several weeks, while developing devices for OpenAI, after discovering an authentication bug that allowed him to tap into Apple’s information.
 
The case is Apple v. Liu, 5:26-cv-07078, US District Court, Northern District of California (San Jose).

data.title: Hackers reportedly breach US Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform
data.description:
Hackers have reportedly gained access to the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing and control platform, marking the latest in a series of cyber intrusions targeting critical US government infrastructure, according to a Reuters exclusive report cited by Fox News on Friday (local time).

According to Fox News, the US Air Force has not publicly confirmed the breach. It also remains unclear who was responsible for the intrusion and whether any data was stolen.

The reported breach comes amid a series of cyber incidents involving US intelligence and law enforcement agencies, including apparent intrusions affecting the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

 

On Tuesday (local time), CNN reported that the CIA and ODNI had suffered an apparent cyberattack affecting unclassified information, citing four sources familiar with the matter.

According to CNN, the intrusion targeted a system used by the agencies for open-source intelligence analysis. Although the full extent of the breach remained unclear, officials maintained that no classified information had been affected.

An ODNI official told CNN that the incident had not disrupted any critical capabilities or classified systems.

Open-source intelligence encompasses commercially available information, including social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. While much of this information is publicly accessible, some is obtained through data vendors and can reveal sensitive details, particularly when combined with other datasets.

The latest developments also follow an apparent cyberattack targeting the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to access criminal records, outstanding warrants and background-check information.

US President Donald Trump appeared to acknowledge the FBI breach during a phone interview with Fox News on November 21.

"I will say that it's not good--I don't like that," Trump said when asked about the incident, which CNN had earlier reported.

According to CNN, the FBI is investigating the intrusion, which marked the second reported breach involving the bureau in recent months.

A former FBI official who had led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN that the NCIC was among the most important information-sharing platforms used by law enforcement agencies, raising concerns that hackers could compromise the reliability of information stored in the database, beyond exposing sensitive records.

The FBI had also faced a separate cyberattack in September, when a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive personal information belonging to bureau employees through a recruitment website.

According to CNN, some FBI employees were left uncertain about whether their personal information had been compromised. A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author was subsequently arrested and faces charges in connection with the breach.

Earlier, in 2023, hackers accessed a computer system used by the FBI's New York field office for investigations into child sexual exploitation. According to CNN, the compromised system included one used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein investigation.

The series of reported intrusions has raised broader concerns over the security of sensitive information and critical systems maintained by US government agencies.

data.title: Bihar's 'Bahubalis' thrive as parties prize winnability over the law
data.description:
A lot of us Indians have been transfixed by the wedding of Bihar strongman and expelled Janata Dal (United) MLA Anant Singh’s daughter. Estimates vary, but it seems between 300,000 and 500,000 people attended the wedding in Mokama. Anant Singh, mind you, is under trial for murder, out on bail, with 27 other serious cases to his name.  
The highlight of the wedding was a horse race with a Thar for the winner, plus much celebration, festivity and unlimited food. TV channels, especially some Hindi channels, have been dining out on this, counting the rasgullas and gulab jamuns on the guests’ plates. I saw one where the guest said he had six of each and complained that the others had collected a dozen or more. The highlight for me, however, was this scene: Anant Singh on a Land Cruiser, in an open black jacket, waving his gamcha (shoulder-wrap) with one hand and twirling his moustache with the other; thousands screaming “chhote Sarkar, chhote Sarkar” (literally, younger master). That’s because his brother Dilip Singh, who died in 2006, was the “bade Sarkar” (the elder master).
 
The “bade Sarkar” passed on the baton flawlessly to his younger brother, making him the leading Bahubali (strongman) of Mokama, among the poorest parts of Bihar. No surprise then that Mokama has been under the sway of not just one Bahubali, but two competing and feuding dynasties. Important fact: Both are from the same (upper) caste, Bhumihar. Both have been much in demand by political parties. In politics anywhere, “winnability” usually is like the Gangajal that washes a candidate of all sins. This is only more pronounced in the Hindi heartland. 
The bade-chhote Sarkar’s rival has been Surajbhan Singh, a former MP but long since banned from contesting after his conviction in a 1992 murder case. It took a fast-track court until 2008 to convict him. But never mind, his wife Veena Devi picked up the mantle. She, too, is a former MP, though lately she’s been losing elections. The rivalry continues. The population is divided in its loyalties between the two dynasties. But, as you’d expect, more would always be on the winning side — Anant Singh’s. 
Let’s keep the focus on the man of the moment, the bride’s father. Anant Singh has led a charmed life. He has faced multiple cases, but nothing takes away his sheen or grip on power. Being in or out of jail doesn’t matter. He was jailed in 2019, for example, under multiple charges including under the draconian UAPA (Unlawful Activities Prevention Act) after at least one AK-47, 22 cartridges and two bombs were recovered from his home. That should’ve finished his political career. Not in Bihar though. 
In the 2020 state elections, he contested from jail and won. And which chief minister doesn’t want any MLA from anywhere to shore up their numbers? In Hindi heartland politics, nobody is immune from it. Not even ever-so-holier-than-cow Nitish Kumar. His government dropped the UAPA charges in the final chargesheet and Anant Singh was out on bail. Just how tightly have you fastened your seatbelts as I recount this story?  
He wouldn’t be Anant Singh if you could keep him away from “adventure” and he always looks well-equipped for it. See the pictures from the wedding, him strutting about in track pants, a zipped-up jacket, with a cowboy hat on his head and flip-flops (hawai chappals) on his feet, surrounded by a dozen-plus henchmen carrying rifles. At the wedding, the only role for the police was in traffic management. 
His latest “adventure” came during the campaign for the Assembly elections in the fall of 2025. In a clash, Dular Chand Yadav of Prashant Kishor’s Jan Suraj Party was killed. Anant Singh was charged for the murder. He campaigned from jail and won. Union Minister Rajiv Ranjan (Lalan) Singh, also from his caste, campaigned for him while he was in jail. That was an IOU.
In the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, Anant Singh fielded his wife, Nilam Devi, against Lalan Singh on a Congress ticket. Of course, she lost. But, by 2024, Anant Singh was campaigning for Lalan Singh in the general elections. If you think this movement from one side to the other is bewildering, it’s because every party loves to have a good “winnable” Bahubali. Now you understand why Lalan Singh campaigned for a former rival who was now jailed. In March this year, the Patna High Court granted him bail. That’s what the Supreme Court has now cancelled. He is to surrender on December 1. But, he’s been telling his crowds not to worry, the Supreme Court will give him bail within three months. 
Let’s stay with Mokama and check out the history of the “chhote-bade Sarkars”. In 1990 and 1995, elder brother Dilip Singh won on Janata Dal tickets. He subsequently became a member of the Legislative Council. 
In 2005 and 2010, Anant Singh won from the older brother’s constituency. In 2015, he left the JD(U), contested as an Independent and still won. The tables turned in 2020, but only in terms of party loyalties. Anant Singh won again, this time from the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD). You don’t need more evidence that everybody needs a Bahubali. Remember, even the Congress had fielded his wife in 2019. 
While the UAPA charges were dropped, Anant Singh was still disqualified as an MLA in 2022 for possessing illegal weapons. This was after his Arms Act conviction by the MP/MLA court. Wife Nilam Devi contested the bye-election from his seat and won, retaining the seat for the RJD. Subsequently, the High Court acquitted Anant Singh under the Arms Act charges.  
Mokama is about 90 km from Patna, and carries a curse of geology. A large part of it is a depression, also described as The Tal (the lake). It’s prone to regular floods even in normal rains. 
Like most of Bihar, its economy is based on remittances. The people young and old that remain, have very little to do. The Bahubalis, therefore, become providers of petty contracts and casual labour in their “real estate” projects, sand-mining (mostly illegal), and generally in manning their wide protection rackets. 
I can take you on a grand gangland tour of the Hindi heartland, but let’s stay with Bihar this week. It gave India one of its most notorious mafiosi, Shahabuddin, the “lord and master” of Siwan. For years, he ran his empire, ordered hits and hostage-taking for ransom from jail, even while serving life-term for murder. But his wife, Hena, and son Osama, now an RJD MLA, have kept the legacy alive. They aren’t politically untouchable. The more striking case, currently in the headlines, is Anand Mohan. The “don of Sheohar” was finally nailed when convicted for the 1994 murder of G Krishnaiah, an IAS officer and then district magistrate of Gopalganj. 
In 2023, Nitish Kumar amended Bihar’s prison remission rules in a manner you could only describe as designed bespoke for Anand Mohan. He lifted the restriction on remission for those convicted of killing public servants on duty. Anand Mohan is now out. It’s only this week that the Supreme Court quashed the Bihar Government’s customised remission policy. 
He will return to jail, like Anant Singh. But, even when he’s been away his wife, Lovely, and son Chetan have been contesting and often winning from the pocket borough. Both have been courted across parties. We could move to Pappu Yadav and his wife Ranjeet Ranjan.  But we will be moving into the territory of what young people call TMI, or too much detail. 
I can take you through the star cast of Bahubalis of neighbouring Uttar Pradesh, from Atiq Ahmed to the Ansaris and Hari Shankar Tiwari. But here’s the larger point: There may be a million problems that bedevil the Hindi Heartland, yet the love of the gangster is among the top three, along with caste and communalism. 
 
By special arrangement with ThePrint

data.title: US urged Venezuela, Iraq to consider leaving OPEC amid oil output push
data.description:
The Trump administration encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC earlier this year and prevented Venezuela from paying its annual membership dues to the group, according to 10 people familiar with the matter.
 
The previously unreported moves targeted two of OPEC’s five founding members, marking an unusually direct challenge to an organisation President Donald Trump has long accused of keeping oil prices artificially high.
 
US officials were pushing for greater oil production and investment in both countries at the time, and some worried OPEC production limits could eventually constrain those ambitions, according to people familiar with the discussions.
 
The US pressure on Venezuela went far enough that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened this summer, persuading the Trump administration not to press the issue further, two people familiar with the matter said.
 
 
In Iraq, Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi raised the possibility of leaving OPEC at a government meeting this summer after discussions with US officials who encouraged the idea, two people familiar with the matter said.
 
Iraq’s oil ministry pushed back, persuading al-Zaidi to keep Iraq in the group and consider seeking a higher production quota instead, the people said.
 
The United States has powerful leverage over both countries. The US controls Venezuela’s access to state funds following the January ouster of Nicolas Maduro, while Iraq’s oil revenues continue to pass through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, a relic of the 2003 Iraq War.
 
The US State Department did not answer questions about whether it had prevented Venezuela from paying its OPEC membership fee. But it confirmed Washington has the power to decide on Venezuela’s use of state funds, now held in a US-controlled account set up after Maduro’s removal.
 
“The Department receives disbursement requests from the interim Venezuelan government and reviews the requests, including against a list of approved and prohibited uses of the foreign Government Deposit Funds,” a State Department official told Reuters.
 
The official said that it was possible that lower-level US officials had raised the question of leaving OPEC with Venezuela’s government earlier this year, but that “it has not been among the issues raised by high-level officials”.
 
The State Department’s conversations with Iraq, meanwhile, “have focused on improving energy infrastructure to increase production and transportation of energy, not OPEC,” the official said.
 
Representatives for OPEC and for the governments of Venezuela, Iraq and Saudi Arabia did not respond to requests for comment.
 
The US manoeuvres add strain to an organisation that has already lost four members since 2019, and whose share of the global oil market recently hit a low on the back of disruptions caused by the US and Israeli war on Iran, another OPEC founding member.
 
“The risk of OPEC fracture is rising,” said Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro.
 
The United Arab Emirates announced its exit from OPEC earlier this year after becoming frustrated with the group’s production caps, while Angola, Ecuador and Qatar quit the group in 2024, 2020 and 2019, respectively. There are no indications the US was involved in those decisions.
 
CUSTOMER TO COMPETITOR
 
OPEC was founded in Baghdad in September 1960 by oil-producing countries seeking to assert more control over a global market that had become dominated by a small handful of Western oil companies.
 
Founded by Iraq, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Venezuela, OPEC is now made up of 11 members. It has also developed an alliance with several other producer countries, including Russia, called OPEC+, which regularly meets to decide on coordinated production levels.
 
Trump has repeatedly attacked OPEC throughout his decades-long business and political career, calling it a cartel and a monopoly profiting from the rest of the world. Over the past decade, though, the US has become the world’s largest oil producer, turning it from an OPEC customer into its main rival for oil market share.
 
After the US seized Maduro in January, the US State Department opened discussions with Venezuelan officials in Washington on whether the country should leave OPEC, five people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
 
They did not identify the individuals who took part in those discussions.
 
Trump wanted US oil majors to revive Venezuela’s oil output — something he said would shore up energy security in the Western Hemisphere — and worried that OPEC policy decisions could hinder that plan, the sources said.
 
Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened, however, persuading the Trump administration not to push further, two of the sources said. Saudi Arabia is OPEC’s top producer and its de facto leader.
 
In August, Trump said it was up to Venezuela whether to leave OPEC.
 
US officials this summer also held talks with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi, encouraging Iraq’s departure from OPEC as US oil majors Exxon Mobil and Chevron planned major new investments there, two people familiar with the matter said.
 
Al-Zaidi later raised the issue at a government meeting. His oil ministry persuaded him to stay and instead potentially seek a higher OPEC quota, they said.
 
The issue could come up again since some elements of Iraq’s ruling coalition are favourable to leaving OPEC and OPEC+, which they view as dominated by Saudi Arabia and Russia, the people said.
 
There is no indication Washington has sought to block Baghdad’s OPEC dues.
 
After the US invasion of Iraq in 2003, the United States began routing Iraq’s oil revenues through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. That structure remains in place more than two decades later.
 
This year, the US threatened to starve Iraq of its oil money if it didn’t cut Iran’s influence in its government.
 
‘MORE IMPORTANT MATTERS’
 
OPEC membership fee payments are typically due in the first quarter of each year and pay for staff salaries, research and travel at the OPEC Secretariat in Vienna.
 
Unlike the United Nations, where dues are scaled to the size of a country’s economy, OPEC splits the fees equally among members at around €2.8 million ($3.08 million) each.
 
The price tag is tiny compared to OPEC oil revenues, but paying it carries symbolic importance as a marker of continued membership in an organisation Caracas helped create.
 
Washington argued money from Venezuela could be spent on more important matters, one of the people familiar with the country’s relationship with OPEC said.
 
OPEC has the discretion to disregard unpaid membership fees and is not planning to expel Venezuela over the issue, two OPEC sources told Reuters.
 
Washington’s control of Venezuela’s oil revenues and finances has led some in the South American country to refer to their country as a US protectorate, instead of a sovereign nation.
 
The US Government Accountability Office opened a formal investigation in July into the administration’s management and disbursement of Venezuelan oil revenues, following congressional requests for transparency.
 
The Trump administration has said Venezuela’s oil revenues are being used to meet the needs of the Venezuelan people, including to pay government salaries and fund essential services.
 
Reuters could not establish exactly when the US rejected the OPEC dues payment request.
 
Venezuela is currently exempt from OPEC+ oil output quotas as its production has collapsed from historical highs due to years of sanctions and mismanagement.
 
The country pumped about 1.2 million barrels per day (bpd) in September, according to OPEC figures. Its state oil company PDVSA has said it plans to reach 1.5 million bpd by the end of next year.
 
OPEC last regulated Caracas’ output with quotas in 2017-18, when the country’s target was around 2 million bpd. The country’s return to the quota system is unlikely until it hits that level again, a source familiar with Venezuela’s OPEC position said.

data.title: IT, bank heavyweights drag markets down 1% amid rising crude oil prices
data.description:
At a time when traders and investors were ready to shake off their worries from rising crude oil prices, they faced a nasty shock on Friday. Brent crude rose towards $98 a barrel on renewed tension in West Asia. The rupee weakened to about 92.99 against the dollar, and domestic bond yields rose to 7.27 per cent, or up 3 basis points (bps). This had a direct negative impact on stock prices. 
The Nifty fell 277.30 points, or 1.07 per cent, to 25,607.20, and the Sensex lost 989.33 points, or 1.17 per cent, to close the day at 83,339.26. The Nifty briefly traded above Thursday’s close before sliding to 25,565.90. Both indices posted their first weekly fall in five weeks, with the Nifty down 0.75 per cent and the Sensex 0.69 per cent. The Nifty is 2.9 per cent below its 52-week high. 
 
Interestingly, what hit the largecaps did not hurt the midcap and smallcap stocks. On the NSE, 1,566 stocks rose and 1,181 fell. The Nifty Smallcap 250 gained 0.53 per cent and the Midcap 150 was flat, even as 40 of the 50 Nifty stocks fell. 
Traders booked profits in information technology (IT) and heavyweight bank stocks on Friday, a day after a sharp IT rally, pulling the Nifty 50 down. 
 
The Nifty IT index fell 1.88 per cent, the most among sectors, giving back about half of Thursday’s 3.66 per cent gain. HCLTech fell 3.03 per cent, Infosys 2.68 per cent, and Tata Consultancy Services slid 2.57 per cent, after rising 4.7-6.4 per cent on Thursday.
The Nifty Bank index fell 0.78 per cent on Friday, and declined 2.47 per cent this week, dragged down by heavyweights HDFC Bank, State Bank of India (SBI), and ICICI Bank. The three banks fell 0.55 per cent, 1.12 per cent, and 1.09 per cent, respectively, from Thursday’s close. Axis Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank fared the worst on Friday, declining 1.98 per cent and 1.95 per cent, respectively. 
Though the selling was confined to the largest lenders, ICICI Bank fell 1.09 per cent and SBI declined 1.12 per cent, losing ₹12,501 crore and ₹11,769 crore in market value, respectively. The two, worth a combined ₹21.8 trillion, make up 10.7 per cent of the Nifty 50’s market value of ₹204.55 trillion, and account for 10.8 per cent of its ₹2.26 trillion fall on Friday.

data.title: ACLU challenges US subpoenas seeking to unmask immigration policy critics
data.description:
The Trump administration is abusing the grand jury process in an effort to unmask social media users anonymously criticising its immigration enforcement tactics, civil rights attorneys claim in a federal court filing Friday.

A federal class action, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union, seeks a court order enjoining the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security from conducting a "bad-faith investigation" that violates the anonymous individuals' First Amendment free speech rights.

The scope of the investigation remains a mystery, but the ACLU says government lawyers have issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas seeking to identify critics and provide their personal information to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement investigators.

 

ACLU attorneys sued on behalf of four unnamed social media users, asking the district court in Washington to block subpoenas seeking account information for users of social media companies, including Meta, Bluesky and X, formerly known as Twitter. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the ACLU case's unsealing on Wednesday.

Boasberg scheduled a January 6 hearing for arguments on the ACLU's request for a preliminary injunction against the government. The administration has until December 14 to respond in writing to the ACLU's allegations.

Spokespeople for DHS and US Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office in Washington didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. Pirro, Attorney General Todd Blanche and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin are named as defendants in the ACLU's lawsuit.

ACLU lawyers say Pirro's office has used the term "Investigation 18" to describe efforts to identify and obtain the personal information.

"The investigation," the ACLU says, "is a bad-faith fishing expedition initiated to gather intrusive intelligence and facilitate retaliation against dissenters." The ACLU says its lawsuit in Washington is the "first systemic civil challenge, and the first case that will be litigated in public view, to the Trump administration's abuse of grand jury unmasking subpoenas." "The government is weaponising the grand jury process to retaliate against people for expressing their political views online," ACLU attorney Laura Moraff said in a statement.

The ACLU argues that the subpoenas to social media platforms are part of a broader pattern of intimidation. DHS has sent hundreds of administrative subpoenas to tech companies in the past year to seek information about online ICE critics, the ACLU says.

The civil rights organisation says the Trump administration has shifted to using grand jury subpoenas - a more secretive process - after encountering pushback to the administrative subpoenas from users and tech companies.

The ACLU lawsuit's plaintiffs include a Bluesky user who wrote about an ICE-related shooting in New York by posting: "Burn ICE to the ground. Burn DHS to the ground. Salt the earth." Another plaintiff is a college student whose posts on X included an expletive directed at DHS, ICE and Trump.

"Defendants' rampant use of subpoenas to unmask critics of the federal government is occurring against the backdrop of repeated suggestions that Defendants are building a database of dissenters," ACLU lawyers wrote.

data.title: Taiwan heads to polls in tight local elections as China watches closely
data.description:
By Rebecca Choong Wilkins and Yian Lee
 
Taiwan heads to the polls Saturday for local elections that could reshape the political field ahead of the 2028 presidential contest, with voters galvanised by an unexpectedly close race in the capital Taipei. 
Some 19.6 million people are eligible to vote for mayors and county chiefs across 22 cities and counties, with more than 11,000 smaller roles up for grabs. Polls run from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., with initial results expected in the evening.
 
The vote will test whether President Lai Ching-te’s Democratic Progressive Party can translate its record run of three straight presidential victories into gains at the local level, where the opposition Kuomintang has long been stronger. For the KMT, which advocates friendlier ties with China, the results could reorder the field of politicians vying to challenge Lai in 2028 — a contest Beijing is closely watching.
 
 
“A poor showing by the KMT would certainly affect Beijing’s calculations going forward,” said Yen Wei-ting, an assistant research fellow at Academia Sinica in Taipei. “It would likely push the KMT to moderate its approach in parliament and move closer to the political center.”
 
Both parties are battling for independent voters. People who don’t identify with or consistently support a particular party account for 30 per cent to 40 per cent of the electorate. They represent the largest and fastest-growing bloc, according to Lev Nachman, an associate professor at National Taiwan University who has researched the island’s political viewpoints for the past decade.
 
“This election is about whether any party could break through the intense political polarisation in the past elections and broaden its appeal among independent voters,” said Austin Wang, an associate professor of political science at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.
 
The positions up for grabs are all in local government, and Wang said that most voters will focus on issues like traffic, food safety, childcare and the cost of living, noting that relations with China played a relatively muted role in 2018 and 2022 local elections. 
In contrast, the quadrennial presidential and legislative elections, next expected in January 2028, typically see more discussion of foreign policy. The ruling DPP advocates self-determination for the democracy and has been ostracised by Beijing, which claims Taiwan is its territory despite the island never having been part of the People’s Republic of China.
 
That tension is why foreign investors will watch Saturday’s results for clues on the coming presidential contest and the broader trajectory for ties with China. Taiwan’s tech-heavy equity market is already under pressure amid doubts over the durability of the global artificial intelligence trade, which is powered by chips made on the island. Overseas funds offloaded about NT$1 trillion ($30.4 billion) of local shares on a net basis in November — putting the market on course for a record monthly outflow, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. 
 
“All eyes will be on the mayor elections in the six special municipalities, including Taipei, New Taipei, Taoyuan, Taichung, Tainan and Kaohsiung, as the results tend to provide a good indicator for the next presidential election about a year away,” UBS Group AG’s sales desk wrote in a note to clients. “KMT government is historically perceived to carry lower cross-strait risks, translating into a reduced geopolitical discount potentially, and vice versa.”
 
The broad economy is performing strongly, though many people feel they’re missing out on the benefits of the AI boom. The statistics bureau on Friday raised its estimate for full-year economic growth to more than 13 per cent, and forecast a 6.5 per cent expansion in 2027, thanks to demand for tech. 
 
It’s not permitted to publish opinion polls in the 10 days before the vote, but the contest attracting the most interest is the capital Taipei, where the DPP hopes to win the mayoralty for the first time since 1994. Puma Shen is challenging KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an in what is seen as a contest between potential future presidential candidates. Four of Taiwan’s five directly elected presidents were previously mayors, with three having led Taipei.
 
A China hawk sanctioned by Beijing, Shen faced an alleged cyberattack targeting his campaign. Wanted by Chinese police for alleged “separatism,” the legislator said he wears a bulletproof vest when traveling overseas. He has also campaigned in a vehicle with bulletproof shields.
 
Chiang studied and practiced law in the US and is claimed to be a great-grandson of Chiang Kai-shek, who lost the Chinese civil war to Mao Zedong’s communists and fled to Taiwan with the remnants of the Republic of China government. He has visited China and met officials there. 
 
In 2022, the KMT won 14 of Taiwan’s 22 cities and counties, compared with five for the DPP, thanks to grassroots networks going back decades. But the DPP is also trying to flip neighboring New Taipei, Taiwan’s most populous municipality, after losing there by almost 25 percentage points in 2022. It is defending Kaohsiung, a longtime DPP stronghold.
 
Voters will separately cast ballots in a nationwide referendum on whether the government should revive nuclear power, though the government is already exploring plans to restart shuttered atomic plants. 
 
Taiwanese elections are the biggest democratic exercise in the Chinese-speaking world and the Stockholm-based Global State of Democracy Initiative, which tracks elections globally, says Taiwan is one of the highest-performing societies in terms of democratic rights, representation, participation and the rule of law.
 
Still, the government has warned of attempts by China to interfere in the elections, including through AI-generated deepfakes, disinformation campaigns, illicit funding and cyberattacks. China has typically stepped up pressure during elections.
 
To ensure transparency and minimise fraud, votes must be cast in person in the area where a person’s household is registered, while ballots are counted publicly. A desire to participate is why Wang, a 35-year-old finance worker living in Singapore, recently traveled to Taipei to vote for the DPP’s Shen — her first time voting in a local election.
 
“This is exciting,” Wang said, declining to give her full name while discussing politics. “It’s the first time we might see change.”

data.title: IndiGo resumes Jeddah, Madinah flights; extends Riyadh, Dammam curbs
data.description:
Indian airline IndiGo has resumed select flight operations to and from Saudi Arabia's Jeddah and Madinah, while extending the suspension of services to Riyadh and Dammam until December 7 amid ongoing regional tensions in Saudi Arabia.

In a travel advisory posted on X, IndiGo said the decision was taken after assessing the prevailing situation and operational considerations.

"Following a careful assessment of the prevailing situation and the associated operational considerations, we are pleased to resume select flight operations to and from Jeddah and Madinah. However, flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam will remain cancelled until 7 December 2026 (inclusive)," the airline said.

 

IndiGo said affected passengers were being notified through their registered contact details and advised travellers to check their flight status on its website or mobile app before heading to the airport.

The Indian Embassy in Riyadh also shared the advisory, confirming the continued suspension of services to the Saudi capital and Dammam.

In a post on X, the Indian Embassy said, "Indigo airlines announces resumption of select flight operations to and from Jeddah and Madinah. However, flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam will remain cancelled until 7 December 2026."

The flight update comes after a Houthi attack on an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia's Jazan region on Thursday killed one person, drawing condemnation from regional organisations and neighbouring countries.

According to Al Jazeera, the Arab League condemned what it called the "repeated terrorist attacks launched by the Houthi militia" against Saudi Arabia, including the strike on the Jazan refinery.

"Targeting oil facilities and vital economic infrastructure constitutes a flagrant violation of the kingdom's sovereignty," the Arab League said in a statement.

Al Jazeera also reported that Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi described the attack as a "dangerous escalation", saying the GCC states stood united with Saudi Arabia in confronting threats to its security and sovereignty.

Qatar, meanwhile, condemned the strike as a "reprehensible act of aggression" and a "clear breach" of international law, Al Jazeera reported.

In a statement, Qatar's Foreign Ministry expressed condolences to the victim's family and voiced support for all "legitimate measures Saudi Arabia takes to safeguard its sovereignty, security, territorial integrity, and interests".

It further said Saudi Arabia's security was an essential part of Qatar's security and the collective security framework of the GCC.

data.title: FSSAI sanctions prosecution against Bisleri again after Bengal sample fails
data.description:
Food regulator FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International after a packaged drinking water sample collected from its West Bengal plant failed laboratory testing, sources said.

The sample tested positive for coliform bacteria, they added.

This form of bacteria can enter water systems through sewage leaks or damaged pipes, among other pathways.

This action marks the second instance of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) sanctioning prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd, a leading player in the packaged drinking water sector in the country.

On Sunday, the FSSAI announced similar legal proceedings after a sample from one of Bisleri's plants in Goa also failed testing.

 

The West Bengal sample was taken from a plant in Jalpaiguri's Telipara village.

The presence of coliform bacteria was confirmed by both primary and referral laboratories. As a result, the FSSAI prohibited the sale of only one specific batch (batch number PB 201) on August 12, 2026, sources stated.

In view of the violations of the food safety rules, FSSAI has granted "sanction for prosecution" against Bisleri International.

Responses from the FSSAI and Bisleri International could not be ascertained immediately.

In the Goa case, the FSSAI had said the "sample was found non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006." Following an appeal from Bisleri, the sample was forwarded to a referral food laboratory, which also classified it as "unsafe" due to detection of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), according to the regulator.

These laboratory findings confirmed violations related to unsafe food practices, which led the FSSAI to initiate prosecution under the Food Safety Act, 2006.

On Monday, Bisleri International asserted that its product is safe for consumption and that the company would cooperate with the FSSAI to address the issues raised.

Earlier this week, FSSAI CEO Rajit Punhani stated that the agency is collecting packaged drinking water samples nationwide, with lab testing for quality expected to be completed within one to two months. He emphasised that enforcement actions aim to ensure compliance, not to create panic.

He noted that the regulator, in the past year, has undertaken enforcement activities for many food as well as beverage products, adding that it would soon start inspection of 'packaging materials' used for food items.

Additionally, the FSSAI has expanded the scope of its scrutiny.

The central regulator has communicated with state food commissioners and regional directors to enhance surveillance, inspection, and sampling of 'packaged drinking water and mineral water.' It also asked them to take action against companies in case of non-compliance.

In this calendar year, the FSSAI has increased enforcement measures against food business operators and e-commerce companies. The regulator has also taken action against manufacturers of energy drinks and alcoholic beverages.
